summary: Defines the Signature Validation Token (SVT), which gives evidence that an electronic signature was valid. Signatures have limited lifetimes for validation, and a trusted authority issues an SVT to assert that a signature was successfully checked according to defined procedures. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Signature checks can expire as keys age. A trusted helper checks one and gives you a signed note saying it was good, so you can prove it later.

questions: what is a signature validation token
how to preserve proof that a signature was valid
how long can a digital signature be validated
subtitle: Proving a signature was valid at a specific time, so it can be verified later without the original.

tldr.problem: Electronic signatures have a limited lifespan: the keys and algorithms used to create them become insecure over time, and the certificates that vouch for the signer may no longer be available. Eventually, an old signature may become impossible to verify with any confidence.
tldr.mechanism: A trusted authority checks the signature, validates the certificate chain, and issues a Signature Validation Token (SVT)—a signed statement that the signature was good at a particular moment. The SVT binds together the signature, the document, the signer's certificate, and proof that validation succeeded.
tldr.outcome: Instead of validating the original signature later (which may be impossible), you can validate the SVT. As long as the SVT itself is trustworthy, the signature is proven valid without needing to revisit the original checks or old algorithms.

today: RFC 9321 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It defines a method for preserving the evidence that a signature was validated, which can help solve the long-term validation problem but does not replace the ETSI standards for archiving signatures.

sections.title: The Challenge of Long-Term Signature Validation
sections.content:
Electronic signatures prove that a document was signed by a particular person at a particular time. But signatures have a problem: they rely on cryptographic algorithms and certificates that become less trustworthy as time passes. Keys may be compromised, algorithms may be broken, and the certificates that authenticated the signer are not kept forever.

Traditional solutions, like the ETSI standards (XAdES, PAdES, CAdES), extend how long a signature can be validated by attaching extra evidence—revocation data, timestamps, archival proofs. This works, but the storage and validation of all that evidence becomes very complex.
sections.eli5: Checking an old signature is like trying to read a receipt from 20 years ago when the store no longer exists and nobody remembers the cashier. You need to keep proof from back then.

sections.title: What a Signature Validation Token Is
sections.content:
An SVT is a signed statement from a trusted authority saying that a particular electronic signature was successfully validated. The authority checks three things: that the signature matches the document, that the signature can be verified by the signer's certificate, and that the signer's certificate is valid through a proper chain to a trusted root.

The SVT captures the result of these checks—passed, failed, or indeterminate—along with the date and time of the check. It also records which validation policy was applied, details about the signer's certificate chain, and evidence of when the signature existed. Once issued, the SVT itself is signed with the authority's private key, making it a piece of evidence that can stand on its own.
sections.eli5: Instead of storing the signature and all its proof, a trusted notary checks everything and gives you a signed note saying 'I checked this on October 18, 2026, and it was good.' You keep that note.

sections.title: Structure of an SVT
sections.content:
An SVT is carried as a JSON Web Token (JWT), a standard format for signed claims. The SVT contains standard JWT claims—an issuer, the time it was issued, and an expiration time—plus custom claims specific to signature validation.

The core claim is sig_val_claims, a SigValidation object that lists all the validated signatures covered by this SVT. For each signature, the SVT records: a hash of the signature value itself (to prove it is the right signature), a hash of what was actually signed (the Signed Bytes), references to all the data that was signed, the signer's certificate or a chain of certificates, the validation result, and optionally the time evidence (such as a timestamp) that proved when the signature existed.

The SVT also specifies which hash algorithm and signature algorithm were used, so a future verifier knows exactly what to trust.
sections.eli5: The SVT is like a sealed envelope with the notary's handwriting. Inside it says 'I checked signature #abc, which signed document XYZ on this date, using this signer's certificate, and the check came back good.'

sections.title: How to Verify a Signature Using an SVT
sections.content:
To verify a signature years later using an SVT, follow these steps: first, locate all available SVTs for the document and signature. Select the most recent SVT that can be successfully validated and meets your requirements. Then verify that the SVT's hashes match the signature value and Signed Bytes you are examining—this proves the SVT applies to your signature, not some other one. Verify that the Signed Data references and hashes match, confirming nothing has changed since the check. Obtain the signer's certificate from the SVT's certificate reference. Finally, verify that the validation result in the SVT—passed, failed, or indeterminate—satisfies your needs.

Notice what you do not do: you do not re-validate the original signature value, and you do not need to run any of the old cryptographic algorithms (unless you want to double-check the SVT itself). This is the key advantage for long-term validation.
sections.eli5: When you need to prove the signature was real, you pull out the notary's note. You check that the note is really from the notary (by verifying their signature), that it matches your document, and that they said it was good. Done.

sections.title: Profiles for Different Signature Types
sections.content:
Signatures come in different forms: XML signatures, PDF signatures, CMS signatures (used in S/MIME email), and JWS signatures (JSON Web Signatures). Each format has its own way of storing data, references, and certificates. An SVT profile defines how to apply the SVT standard to each format—how to reference the signature and document data, how to embed the SVT in the signed format, and how to extract the signer's certificate.

RFC 9321 defines three profiles: one for XML signatures, one for PDF signatures, and one for JWS. Other RFCs or standards may define profiles for additional formats. Each profile ensures that an SVT can be created and verified consistently within its format while remaining compatible with the core SVT specification.
sections.eli5: The SVT is like a standard note, but you write it in different ways depending on whether you are attaching it to a Word document, a PDF, or an email signature.

sections.title: Security and Reliability
sections.content:
An SVT is only as strong as the algorithms and key that protect it. If the private key used to sign the SVT is compromised, or if the algorithm becomes broken, the SVT loses its value. To mitigate this risk, an authority can issue multiple SVTs for the same signature, each signed with different algorithms or key lengths—so that even if one algorithm fails, others remain secure. Alternatively, the authority can reissue SVTs with fresh keys and stronger algorithms before the old ones expire.

A relying party that trusts an SVT should still verify that the SVT's hashes and certificate references match the document being validated. This ensures the SVT actually applies to the document at hand and was not swapped or mixed up. Even if relying entirely on the SVT's validation conclusion, this integrity check is essential.
sections.eli5: A notary's note is only good if you trust the notary. If the notary's stamp is faked or the notary goes out of business, the note is worthless. To be extra safe, you can get notes from multiple notaries.
